query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid solidification combined with controlled thermomechanical annealing refines the eutectic lamellar spacing and increases interphase coherence in eutectic high-entropy alloys, thereby simultaneously enhancing both strength and ductility compared to conventionally cast counterparts.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with relatively coarse lamellar microstructure consisting of soft fcc and hard B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Apply rapid solidification to achieve a fine initial microstructure followed by a controlled thermomechanical processing route (e.g., cold rolling with subsequent annealing) that further refines lamellar spacing and promotes interphase connectivity.
generation.conditions: Tested under standard room-temperature uniaxial tensile conditions with processing parameters (cooling rate, deformation strain, annealing temperature/time) optimized for minimal defects and maximum microstructural refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced interlamellar spacing and enhanced phase connectivity between fcc and B2 phases in the eutectic structure.
generation.mechanism: The intervention increases the effective interphase boundary area, promoting better load transfer and inhibiting premature crack nucleation; this results in strain hardening that boosts yield strength while maintaining or even improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A statistically significant increase in both yield strength and tensile ductility relative to alloys processed by conventional casting, due to the refined and more coherent eutectic microstructure.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloys produced by conventional casting without the rapid solidification and controlled thermomechanical treatment.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only when processing parameters (cooling rate, degree of deformation, annealing temperature and time) are carefully optimized. Outside these optimal conditions, excessive defects or over-processing could negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement is supported, the exact magnitude of the strength and ductility enhancement requires experimental determination and may vary with alloy composition and processing precision.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens: one set produced by conventional casting and one set processed with rapid solidification followed by cold rolling and annealing under optimized conditions. Perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests and microstructural analyses on both sets.
measurements: Lamellar spacing and phase coherence via microscopy (e.g., SEM, TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant, simultaneous increase in both strength and ductility compared to the conventionally cast specimens, or if the expected microstructural refinement (reduced lamellar spacing and improved interphase coherence) is not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. chosen.technique: rapid solidification combined with controlled thermomechanical annealing (e.g., post-solidification cold rolling followed by annealing)
chosen.conditions: tested on eutectic high-entropy alloys under standard room-temperature uniaxial tensile conditions
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by providing a single, experimentally accessible processing intervention that refines the eutectic microstructure. Prior studies have noted that either strength or ductility can be improved when one aspect of the microstructure is targeted; by refining the lamellar spacing and enhancing interphase coherence via a controlled cooling and deformation protocol, the expected synergistic effect can be achieved. This intervention is well within standard techniques in materials science and allows a clear test of the hypothesis that improved microstructural architecture can simultaneously boost strength and ductility.
